chapterTitle: Deep Dive into CloudWatch Logs and Events
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 15-minute interactive lab walkthrough video. Begin by demonstrating the CloudWatch Logs console, explaining log groups, log streams, and retention policies. Guide learners through installing and configuring the CloudWatch Agent on a pre-launched EC2 instance to send Apache access logs. Show how to generate traffic and verify logs in the console. Next, walk through creating a CloudWatch Logs metric filter to count 5xx errors from the Apache logs. Finally, demonstrate creating an EventBridge rule with a specific event pattern to capture EC2 instance state changes (e.g., `stopped`) and send a notification via SNS. Include clear terminal commands, browser views, and a step-by-step guide for the hands-on activity. End with a reflection prompt asking learners to consider other use cases for EventBridge.

screens.title: Deep Dive into CloudWatch Logs and Events
screens.narratorSegment: Logs tell the operational story that raw metrics often miss. In this lesson you'll learn how CloudWatch Logs collects and organizes log data into log groups and log streams, how to use the CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 or on-premises systems, and how to turn patterns inside logs into numerical metrics with metric filters. You will also learn how Amazon EventBridge (previously CloudWatch Events) routes events to targets and how to write event patterns to trigger automated actions. Together, these services let you centralize diagnostic data, create alerts from real application behavior, and automate responses to infrastructure changes. For example, you can send Apache access logs to a log group, create a metric filter that counts 5xx responses, and then alarm or trigger remediation when the error rate spikes. We'll also discuss retention policies and common mistakes like forgetting retention or using overly broad event patterns. By the end you should be able to configure the agent, define metric filters, and author EventBridge rules that reliably automate operational tasks.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: This screen connects objectives to concrete operational tasks you'll perform as a SysOps Administrator. First, understanding log groups and streams lets you organize logs by application or resource and apply a retention policy that balances audit needs and cost. For example, set a longer retention for security logs and a shorter one for high-volume debug logs. Second, configuring the CloudWatch Agent enables collection of logs and system metrics not available by default; you'll create a JSON config that points files to a log group and names streams using the instance ID. Third, metric filters let you turn textual patterns into numeric signals. For instance, a filter that matches 5xx responses can create a metric you then use in an alarm to notify developers. Lastly, EventBridge rules automate responses: you can trigger a Lambda to run when an EC2 instance stops or schedule nightly maintenance with a cron rule. Understanding these outcomes prepares you to centralize logs, detect problems, and automate remediation in a repeatable way.

screens.title: CloudWatch Logs Architecture
screens.narratorSegment: CloudWatch Logs organizes log data in a two-level structure. At the top are log groups, which are logical containers for related logs. You assign retention, tags, metric filters, and access controls at the log group level. Inside each log group are log streams: a stream represents a sequence of log events from a specific source, such as one EC2 instance, a single Lambda function, or a particular application process. Each log event is a timestamped message. Understanding this structure helps you design for scale and cost. For example, grouping all web application access logs under a single log group lets you apply one retention policy and a consistent set of metric filters. A common mistake is using too many small log groups without need, which increases management overhead, or conversely putting unrelated logs together so a single retention policy deletes different apps' history. Another practical point: retention policies are set on log groups. If you need different retention per source, use separate log groups. Think about who needs access and what data must be kept for audits. In short, design log groups and streams to map to ownership, retention requirements, and the patterns you intend to monitor.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › CloudWatch Logs Architecture
Structure and intent
How log groups and streams represent ownership and sequence.
Log Group
Logical container for related streams. Apply retention and access policies here.
Log Stream
A sequence of timestamped events from one source, such as an instance or function.
Log Event
A timestamp and a message. Metric filters inspect the message for patterns.
Common mistake
Using a single log group for unrelated systems, which makes retention and access control blunt instruments and risks deleting important history.
Key Takeaway
Design groups by ownership and retention, streams by source, and keep filter use in mind when grouping.
Architecture Visual
Example mapping
/aws/webapp/access → streams per instance ID; /aws/db/errors → streams per host.
Log event sample
[timestamp] 2026-09-25T12:34:56Z - 203.0.113.12 "GET /index.html" 200 512
[timestamp] 2026-09-25T12:35:01Z - 203.0.113.12 "GET /missing" 404 123
[timestamp] 2026-09-25T12:35:10Z - 203.0.113.12 "POST /api" 500 2048
Why this matters
  • Retention policies are applied at the log group, so plan group boundaries accordingly.
  • Streams make source-level ordering and troubleshooting easier.
  • Metric filters operate on events; clear grouping helps filter scope and manage costs.

screens.title: Retention Policies
screens.narratorSegment: A retention policy determines how long CloudWatch retains log events in a log group before deleting them. This setting is critical for balancing compliance, troubleshooting capability, and cost. Longer retention helps with audits and post-incident investigations, while shorter retention controls storage costs for high-volume applications. For example, you might keep security-related logs for a year but only retain debug logs for thirty days. A common operational pitfall is not setting any retention policy, which leaves logs to grow indefinitely and can produce unexpectedly large storage bills. Another mistake is setting overly aggressive retention and losing historical evidence needed for compliance or root-cause analysis. When planning retention, consider regulatory requirements, your team's debugging needs, and the log volume. You can change retention later, but deletion is irreversible for events past the retention window. As a practical rule, categorize logs by importance and set retention at the group level to simplify management and cost forecasting. Retention Policies means set retention by log group based on compliance and troubleshooting needs; avoid default unlimited retention unless intentional.. In practical terms, how long to keep logs and the operational trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Retention Policies
Retention policy essentials
Define how long to keep logs and why retention is a policy decision, not just a technical setting.
Decide by purpose
Security, compliance, and audit logs usually need longer retention than debug traces.
Cost awareness
Long retention increases storage cost; plan for expected ingestion volume and retention windows.
Change vs delete
Changing retention prevents future deletion; events already deleted are unrecoverable.
Common mistake
Leaving log groups without explicit retention or applying the same retention to all groups without considering business needs.
Practical setup
Example retention plan
  • Security logs: 365 days
  • Application errors: 90 days
  • Debug traces: 30 days
CLI note
# Example: set retention to 90 days for a log group
aws logs put-retention-policy --log-group-name /aws/myapp/errors --retention-in-days 90
Key Takeaway
Retention must balance compliance and cost; design groups to reflect retention needs.

screens.title: CloudWatch Agent: Install and Configure
screens.narratorSegment: The CloudWatch Agent is a lightweight process that collects system metrics and application logs and publishes them to CloudWatch. Installing it on an EC2 instance typically follows these steps: update packages, install the agent package provided for your distribution, create a configuration file that lists files to collect and their destination log group and stream, and then start the agent. The configuration is usually a JSON file that identifies paths, timestamps formats, and log group and stream names. A practical example is collecting Apache access logs: point the agent at /var/log/httpd/access_log, set the log_group_name to "/aws/httpd/access", and use the instance ID for the stream name so each host has its own stream. Make sure the EC2 instance role includes logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents. If logs do not appear, check the agent log file under /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs for parsing errors or permission denials. This flow ensures your logs flow reliably into CloudWatch and remain searchable for metric extraction later. CloudWatch Agent: Install and Configure means install the agent, provide a json config mapping files to log groups and streams, and ensure iam permissions and agent logs are checked when troubleshooting.. In practical terms, install the agent and author the json config to collect apache logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › CloudWatch Agent: Install and Configure
Install and configure
A terminal-first walkthrough for configuring the agent to send Apache access logs.
Terminal — install and start
sudo yum update -y
sudo yum install -y amazon-cloudwatch-agent
# fetch or create config and then start the agent
sudo /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/amazon-cloudwatch-agent-ctl -a fetch-config -m ec2 -c file:/opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/bin/config.json -s
Agent config (excerpt)
{
  "logs": {
    "logs_collected": {
      "files": {
        "collect_list": [
          {
            "file_path": "/var/log/httpd/access_log",
            "log_group_name": "/aws/httpd/access",
            "log_stream_name": "{instance_id}",
            "timestamp_format": "%d/%b/%Y:%H:%M:%S %z"
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}
Example
Configure the agent with /var/log/httpd/access_log and name the stream by instance ID so each host's traffic is isolated for analysis.
Troubleshooting & tips
Check agent logs
Look at /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.log for permission or parsing errors.
IAM role needs
Grant logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents to the instance role.
Common mistake
Pointing to the wrong file path or missing timestamp_format causes parsing issues and dropped events.
Check your understanding
If logs don't appear, what three places do you check? (agent log, IAM role, config file paths)

screens.title: IAM Permissions and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: The CloudWatch Agent writes log events on behalf of an instance, so the instance's IAM role must grant it permissions to manage log groups and streams and to put events. Key permissions include logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents. Without them the agent may fail silently or generate errors in its own log file. When logs do not appear in CloudWatch, take a few methodical troubleshooting steps. First, verify that the agent process is running on the host. Second, inspect the agent log at /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs/amazon-cloudwatch-agent. log for error messages such as permission denied or parsing failures. Third, confirm the configured file path exists and that the agent user can read it. Fourth, check that the target log group name is correct and that retention or access policies aren't blocking creation. A useful diagnostic is to simulate a log write locally and watch the agent log for an attempt to deliver the event. Remember that many issues stem from permissions or mismatched paths rather than the agent itself, so focus on IAM role policies and file-system access during troubleshooting. IAM Permissions and Troubleshooting means verify agent process, inspect agent logs, confirm iam permissions, and validate file paths to resolve missing log deliveries.. In practical terms, what the agent needs and how to diagnose missing logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Metric Filters
screens.narratorSegment: Metric filters let you convert textual log matches into numerical CloudWatch metrics. You define a filter pattern using a simplified syntax, map it to a metric namespace and name, and set a metric value to emit when a log event matches. This is essential when your application emits only textual signals, like "ERROR" or an HTTP 5xx status, and you want that information in dashboards or alarms. For example, create a filter with pattern [ip, user, request, status_code=5*, size] to count 5xx responses from Apache logs and emit a metric named 5xxErrorCount in namespace MyApplicationMetrics. Each match increments the metric by the specified value, often 1. After the metric exists, use it for CloudWatch Alarms or graphs. Common misconceptions include expecting metric filters to search across multiple log groups automatically; filters are defined per log group and only evaluate events in that group. Also remember that overly broad patterns generate noisy metrics; test patterns in a non-production group before enabling alarms. Metric Filters means define a pattern per log group to count or measure occurrences in logs; use those metrics for alarms and dashboards.. In practical terms, extract numerical metrics from log patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Metric Filters
Pattern → Metric
Define filter patterns, set namespace and metric name, and emit values on matches.
Example filter pattern
Filter pattern: [ip, user, request, status_code=5*, size]
Metric namespace: MyApplicationMetrics
Metric name: 5xxErrorCount
Metric value: 1
Behavior
  • Each matching event emits the metric value chosen.
  • Metrics are created in the specified namespace and available like other CloudWatch metrics.
  • Metric filters are evaluated per log group.
Practical notes
Test patterns
Validate patterns with sample log events before creating alarms to avoid noisy alerts.
Scope
Filters apply to a single log group; use separate filters for different groups as needed.
Check your understanding
Why create a metric filter rather than just searching logs? Because numeric metrics can be graphed, alerted on, and integrated into alarms.

screens.title: From Filter to Alarm
screens.narratorSegment: Once a metric filter emits a custom metric, treat it like any other CloudWatch metric. You can visualize it in dashboards, set alarms on thresholds, or combine it with other metrics for composite alarms. A concrete example: after creating a 5xxErrorCount metric you can create an alarm that fires if the count exceeds 10 within a 5-minute period. That alarm can trigger an SNS topic or a Lambda for remediation. Important differences to remember: metric filters are evaluated per log event and emit values, while alarms operate on aggregated metric data across a time period. A misconception is believing the filter itself will send notifications; it does not. Instead, the metric it generates is what alarms monitor. Also consider data resolution and charges: custom metrics may have different storage and resolution characteristics. Finally, test your end-to-end flow — generate example 5xx responses and confirm the metric appears in the namespace and the alarm transitions to ALARM as expected. From Filter to Alarm means metric filters create metrics; alarms act on those metrics. test the full pipeline from log event to notification to ensure reliable alerts.. In practical terms, use custom metrics in cloudwatch alarms and dashboards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.narratorSegment: Amazon EventBridge is a serverless event bus service that routes events from AWS services, SaaS integrations, and custom applications to targets like Lambda, SNS, SQS, and Step Functions. Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Amazon EventBridge Fundamentals
EventBridge building blocks
Events, buses, rules, patterns, and targets work together to build event-driven automation.
Event
A JSON payload that describes a state change or custom occurrence.
Rule
Matches events using an event pattern and forwards them to targets.
Target
An AWS service or resource invoked when a rule matches an event.
Example rule
Pattern to match EC2 stopped
{
  "source": ["aws.ec2"],
  "detail-type": ["EC2 Instance State-change Notification"],
  "detail": { "state": ["stopped"] }
}
Target example
Send to an SNS topic to notify admins or a Lambda to trigger cleanup.
Misconception
EventBridge does not read log files directly; it routes events emitted by services, scheduled rules, or custom PutEvents calls.

screens.title: Authoring Effective Event Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Event patterns are JSON objects that specify which parts of incoming events must match for a rule to fire. Key fields include source, detail-type, and the nested detail object where resource-specific fields live. Be intentional: broad patterns like matching only source can cause many targets to be invoked unnecessarily, while overly specific patterns risk missing events due to small differences in payload fields. A practical approach is to use schema discovery or sample events from the console to learn the exact fields available, then write patterns that match meaningful changes. For instance, match EC2 instance state-change notifications where detail. state equals stopped to trigger cleanup. Test rules using a non-production bus or by replaying sample events. Also, remember scheduled rules use cron or rate expressions and are a different rule type; they do not require pattern matching. Finally, implement safe targets: for automated remediation, prefer idempotent Lambdas and include safeguards to avoid cascading changes triggered by many similar events. Authoring Effective Event Patterns means use schema discovery and sample events to craft patterns that are neither too broad nor too narrow; test thoroughly before production.. In practical terms, match precisely to avoid missed events or noisy triggers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. fullNarratorScript:
Logs tell the operational story that raw metrics often miss. In this lesson you'll learn how CloudWatch Logs collects and organizes log data into log groups and log streams, how to use the CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 or on-premises systems, and how to turn patterns inside logs into numerical metrics with metric filters. You will also learn how Amazon EventBridge (previously CloudWatch Events) routes events to targets and how to write event patterns to trigger automated actions. Together, these services let you centralize diagnostic data, create alerts from real application behavior, and automate responses to infrastructure changes. For example, you can send Apache access logs to a log group, create a metric filter that counts 5xx responses, and then alarm or trigger remediation when the error rate spikes. We'll also discuss retention policies and common mistakes like forgetting retention or using overly broad event patterns. By the end you should be able to configure the agent, define metric filters, and author EventBridge rules that reliably automate operational tasks.

These four objectives guide our hands-on and conceptual focus. First, you will explain CloudWatch Logs architecture by naming log groups, log streams, and the role of retention settings. You'll be able to describe why grouping streams matters for access control and cost. Second, you'll configure the CloudWatch Agent on EC2 or on-premises servers using a JSON configuration file to collect application and system logs, and ensure the instance role has the proper permissions. Third, you'll use CloudWatch Logs metric filters to search log text and emit custom numerical metrics, such as counting 5xx responses or occurrences of the word "ERROR," and then use those metrics for alarms or dashboards. Fourth, you'll understand EventBridge and author rules with appropriate event patterns to route service or scheduled events to targets like Lambda or SNS. Each objective links concept to practice: for example, configuring a metric filter and then creating an alarm demonstrates end-to-end monitoring. These objectives help you prioritize compliance, cost, observability, and automation as you work through the lab steps.

This screen connects objectives to concrete operational tasks you'll perform as a SysOps Administrator. First, understanding log groups and streams lets you organize logs by application or resource and apply a retention policy that balances audit needs and cost. For example, set a longer retention for security logs and a shorter one for high-volume debug logs. Second, configuring the CloudWatch Agent enables collection of logs and system metrics not available by default; you'll create a JSON config that points files to a log group and names streams using the instance ID. Third, metric filters let you turn textual patterns into numeric signals. For instance, a filter that matches 5xx responses can create a metric you then use in an alarm to notify developers. Lastly, EventBridge rules automate responses: you can trigger a Lambda to run when an EC2 instance stops or schedule nightly maintenance with a cron rule. Understanding these outcomes prepares you to centralize logs, detect problems, and automate remediation in a repeatable way.

CloudWatch Logs organizes log data in a two-level structure. At the top are log groups, which are logical containers for related logs. You assign retention, tags, metric filters, and access controls at the log group level. Inside each log group are log streams: a stream represents a sequence of log events from a specific source, such as one EC2 instance, a single Lambda function, or a particular application process. Each log event is a timestamped message. Understanding this structure helps you design for scale and cost. For example, grouping all web application access logs under a single log group lets you apply one retention policy and a consistent set of metric filters. A common mistake is using too many small log groups without need, which increases management overhead, or conversely putting unrelated logs together so a single retention policy deletes different apps' history. Another practical point: retention policies are set on log groups. If you need different retention per source, use separate log groups. Think about who needs access and what data must be kept for audits. In short, design log groups and streams to map to ownership, retention requirements, and the patterns you intend to monitor.

A retention policy determines how long CloudWatch retains log events in a log group before deleting them. This setting is critical for balancing compliance, troubleshooting capability, and cost. Longer retention helps with audits and post-incident investigations, while shorter retention controls storage costs for high-volume applications. For example, you might keep security-related logs for a year but only retain debug logs for thirty days. A common operational pitfall is not setting any retention policy, which leaves logs to grow indefinitely and can produce unexpectedly large storage bills. Another mistake is setting overly aggressive retention and losing historical evidence needed for compliance or root-cause analysis. When planning retention, consider regulatory requirements, your team's debugging needs, and the log volume. You can change retention later, but deletion is irreversible for events past the retention window. As a practical rule, categorize logs by importance and set retention at the group level to simplify management and cost forecasting. Retention Policies means set retention by log group based on compliance and troubleshooting needs; avoid default unlimited retention unless intentional.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The CloudWatch Agent is a lightweight process that collects system metrics and application logs and publishes them to CloudWatch. Installing it on an EC2 instance typically follows these steps: update packages, install the agent package provided for your distribution, create a configuration file that lists files to collect and their destination log group and stream, and then start the agent. The configuration is usually a JSON file that identifies paths, timestamps formats, and log group and stream names. A practical example is collecting Apache access logs: point the agent at /var/log/httpd/access_log, set the log_group_name to "/aws/httpd/access", and use the instance ID for the stream name so each host has its own stream. Make sure the EC2 instance role includes logs:CreateLogGroup, logs:CreateLogStream, and logs:PutLogEvents. If logs do not appear, check the agent log file under /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/logs for parsing errors or permission denials. This flow ensures your logs flow reliably into CloudWatch and remain searchable for metric extraction later.
